title: Gliese 710 Close Stellar Encounter
shortDescription: A star will pass extremely close to the Solar System, triggering a massive comet storm — in about 1.29 million years.
mainDescription: The star Gliese 710 is expected to make an unusually close passage by the Solar System in about 1.3 million years, approaching to within roughly 0.166 light-years of the Sun. Although still far beyond the planets, the star is projected to pass directly through the outer region of the Oort Cloud — the vast reservoir of icy bodies surrounding the Solar System. Its gravity is expected to disturb billions of dormant comets, altering their orbits and sending some of them inward toward the Sun over the millions of years that follow. Astronomers consider Gliese 710 one of the most significant predicted stellar encounters for the future Solar System because of its unusually close approach. The event will not threaten Earth directly, but it could dramatically increase the number of long-period comets entering the inner Solar System, potentially changing the appearance of Earth’s skies for distant future civilizations.
whatYoullSee: A bright new star moving noticeably across the sky over decades, accompanied by a dramatic increase in bright comets and fireballs for thousands of years.
whyItMatters: One of the closest stellar flybys in millions of years and a major gravitational event for the entire Solar System.
keyFacts: Strong disturbance of the Oort cloud
nextOccurrences: No closer stellar encounters expected for many millions of years.

title: Eta Carinae Hypernova Explosion
shortDescription: The unstable massive star Eta Carinae explodes as a hypernova — within the next 2 million years.
mainDescription: Eta Carinae — one of the most massive and unstable stars in the Milky Way — is expected to end its life in an enormous stellar explosion sometime within the next few million years. Located about 7,500 light-years from Earth, the system contains stars so luminous and energetic that they already rank among the most extreme known objects in the galaxy. In the 19th century, Eta Carinae briefly became one of the brightest stars in the sky during a violent eruption that expelled vast clouds of gas still visible today. When the star finally collapses, it may produce either an exceptionally powerful supernova or even a hypernova, releasing more energy in a short time than the Sun will emit over its entire lifetime. For observers on Earth, the explosion could become bright enough to remain visible in the daytime sky for weeks or months despite its immense distance. Although dramatic on a galactic scale, Eta Carinae is far enough away that the event is not expected to pose a direct threat to Earth.
whatYoullSee: An extremely bright new star in the southern sky, potentially visible even during the day for weeks or months.
whyItMatters: One of the most powerful stellar explosions observable from Earth in millions of years.
nextOccurrences: Events of this scale are extremely rare on million-year timescales.

title: Complete Dissolution of Familiar Constellations
shortDescription: All current constellations will become completely unrecognizable due to stellar motion — in about 5 million years.
mainDescription: Over the next several million years, the familiar constellations of Earth’s night sky will gradually dissolve as stars continue moving through the Milky Way. Although constellations appear fixed on human timescales, every visible star is traveling through space with its own velocity and direction. Over immense periods of time, these slow motions — known as proper motion — steadily reshape the patterns seen from Earth. Familiar formations such as Orion, Ursa Major, Cassiopeia, and Scorpius will become distorted beyond recognition, while entirely new constellations emerge in their place. Some bright stars will drift far apart, others will move closer together, and a few may disappear from naked-eye visibility entirely. The night sky of the distant future will therefore look profoundly different from the one known throughout human history. The event is a reminder that even the seemingly permanent structure of the heavens is temporary when viewed across cosmic timescales.
whatYoullSee: A night sky that looks completely alien to modern observers.
whyItMatters: The total transformation of the human celestial heritage.
nextOccurrences: New constellations will form over tens of millions of years.

title: Sirius Extremely Close Approach
shortDescription: Sirius will pass very close to the Solar System, becoming the brightest star in the sky — in about 6 million years.
mainDescription: Sirius, currently the brightest star visible in Earth’s night sky, is expected to make a much closer approach to the Solar System in about six million years. As the star moves through the Milky Way, its distance from the Sun will gradually shrink to roughly 1.6 light-years — far closer than its present distance of about 8.6 light-years. At that range, Sirius would appear dramatically brighter than it does today, dominating the night sky with an intensity unlike almost any star seen in human history. Future observers on Earth could see Sirius casting noticeable shadows at night and shining with a brilliance rivaling some planets. The star’s blue-white light would become one of the most prominent features of the future sky, altering the appearance of Earth’s constellations and nighttime landscape. The encounter reflects the slow but continuous motion of stars through the galaxy, where even the nearest stellar neighbors gradually change over millions of years.
whatYoullSee: Sirius shining with exceptional brilliance, far outshining all other stars in the night sky.
whyItMatters: One of the closest approaches of a bright star in millions of years.
nextOccurrences: Sirius will gradually move away afterward.

title: Major Comet Bombardment Period
shortDescription: A prolonged period of intense comet impacts on the inner planets — in about 15 million years.
mainDescription: The Solar System may experience a prolonged period of elevated comet activity around 15 million years in the future, potentially increasing the number of large impacts on planets and moons. Over long timescales, gravitational disturbances from passing stars, galactic tides, and earlier stellar encounters can alter the orbits of distant icy bodies in the Oort Cloud, sending larger numbers of comets toward the inner Solar System. During periods of intensified influx, Earth, Mars, and other worlds could face a substantially higher frequency of impacts than they do today. Such episodes would unfold over thousands or even millions of years rather than as a single catastrophic event. Many incoming comets would remain harmless, but some could become bright naked-eye objects in Earth’s sky before passing close to the Sun or colliding with planetary surfaces. Although the exact scale of future bombardment periods remains uncertain, astronomers consider fluctuations in long-period comet activity a natural consequence of the Solar System’s motion through the galaxy and its interactions with the surrounding stellar environment.
whatYoullSee: Frequent bright comets in the sky and possible visible impact events on the Moon and planets.
whyItMatters: A rare period of heightened cosmic danger and spectacular celestial displays.
nextOccurrences: Such intense bombardment periods are rare over long timescales.

title: Permanent Disappearance of Saturn’s Rings
shortDescription: Saturn’s magnificent rings will vanish forever — in about 200 million years.
mainDescription: Saturn’s iconic rings are expected to gradually disappear over the next few hundred million years, eventually leaving the planet without the feature that has defined its appearance for human civilization. Although the rings appear stable and permanent on human timescales, they are made mostly of countless particles of ice and dust orbiting Saturn under delicate gravitational conditions. Observations already show that material from the rings is slowly falling into the planet through a process known as “ring rain,” while gravitational interactions with Saturn’s moons continue to reshape and disperse the system. Over immense stretches of time, these processes are expected to thin the rings until they can no longer remain visible. Future observers in the distant Solar System would see Saturn not as the bright ringed world familiar today, but as a comparatively plain gas giant with little trace of its former structure. The disappearance of the rings is a reminder that even some of the most recognizable features in the Solar System are temporary on cosmic timescales.
whatYoullSee: Saturn transformed into a featureless yellowish orb, losing one of the most beautiful features in the Solar System.
whyItMatters: The permanent end of Saturn’s rings as we know them.
nextOccurrences: Saturn will remain ringless for billions of years.

title: Chaotic Evolution of the Solar System
shortDescription: The orbits of the planets become chaotic and unstable — in about 500 million years.
mainDescription: Over extremely long timescales, the orderly motion of the planets may gradually become less stable as tiny gravitational interactions accumulate throughout the Solar System. Although planetary orbits appear predictable on human timescales, the Solar System is governed by a complex gravitational system in which even very small perturbations can slowly amplify over hundreds of millions or billions of years. Computer simulations suggest that this chaotic evolution could eventually alter the shapes and orientations of planetary orbits in unpredictable ways. In the most extreme scenarios, some planets or moons could experience close encounters, collisions, or even ejection from the Solar System entirely. Mercury is considered especially vulnerable to long-term orbital instability, which in certain simulations can trigger wider disruptions affecting the inner planets. While the probability of catastrophic instability remains low within the near future of the Solar System, the possibility illustrates that planetary systems are not perfectly permanent structures, but dynamic systems evolving across immense cosmic timescales.
whatYoullSee: Gradual but dramatic shifts in the positions and brightness of planets over geological time.
whyItMatters: The beginning of the end of the stable Solar System we know today.
nextOccurrences: The Solar System will never return to its current stable configuration.

title: The Last Total Solar Eclipse on Earth
shortDescription: Total solar eclipses will cease forever as the Moon moves too far away — in about 600 million years.
mainDescription: Total solar eclipses on Earth are expected to come to an end in roughly 600 million years as the Moon continues slowly moving away from our planet. The Moon is currently drifting away from Earth at a rate of about 3.8 centimeters per year due to tidal interactions between Earth and the Moon. Over immense periods of time, this gradual recession will cause the Moon to appear slightly smaller in Earth’s sky until it can no longer completely cover the Sun during an eclipse. After that point, future eclipses will only produce annular eclipses, where a bright ring of sunlight remains visible around the Moon’s silhouette. The dramatic moments of totality — when the Sun’s corona becomes visible and daytime briefly turns to twilight — will disappear permanently from Earth. The existence of total solar eclipses depends on a remarkable coincidence: the Sun and Moon currently appear almost the same size in Earth’s sky despite their enormous difference in actual size and distance. That balance is temporary, making total solar eclipses a relatively brief phenomenon in Earth’s long history.
whatYoullSee: The final perfect alignment where the Moon completely hides the Sun one last time.
whyItMatters: The end of one of the most spectacular natural phenomena in the Solar System.
keyFacts: Caused by tidal recession of the Moon
nextOccurrences: Total solar eclipses will never occur again.
